title: Build an expense policy rule engine
blurb: Build the engine that checks expense reports against company policy, like Rippling's Software Engineer AI pairing question: rules written as data, then trip totals, then daily limits per employee. Each level unlocks when the last one passes.
brief: Finance writes the company's expense policy as a list of rules, plain data like { id: "meal-cap", type: "max_amount", where: { expenseType: "meals" }, limit: "75.00" }, and wants an engine that checks a batch of expenses against it. Build it in rules.js, in three levels: only level 1 is shown now. When every visible test passes, the next level unlocks with new rule types and new tests, and everything from earlier levels must keep working, so a design where a new rule type is a small addition saves you time later. money.js works. Every expense looks like { id: "e1", tripId: "t1", employeeId: "ana", expenseType: "meals", vendorType: "restaurant", vendorName: "Joe's", amountUsd: "49.99", spentAt: "2026-03-02T19:30:00-05:00" } (tripId may be missing). Expenses come from the expense system and are always well-formed, but rules are typed by hand, so check them. Hidden tests for each level you reach run when you finish.
requirements: createEngine(rules) in rules.js checks the rules and returns an engine; engine.evaluate(expenses) returns the list of violations and changes neither its input nor the engine, so it can be called again with other expenses.

Every rule has an id (a non-empty string, unique in the list), a type, and an optional where. A rule applies to an expense when the expense matches every field in where: a string must equal that field of the expense exactly, and an array of strings matches any of them. No where, or {}, applies to every expense.
type "deny": every expense the rule applies to is a violation (for example where: { expenseType: ["airfare", "entertainment"] }).

type "max_amount" with a limit (a dollar string): an expense the rule applies to is a violation when its amount is over the limit. Exactly the limit is allowed. Compare amounts in cents (toCents in money.js), never as strings or floats.

A violation is { ruleId, expenseIds }, where expenseIds is the list of the expenses involved (one, for these rule types). evaluate returns them in rule order, and for one rule in the order of the expenses.

A policy that cannot be enforced as written must fail loudly: createEngine throws RangeError for a rules value that is not an array, a missing or duplicate id, an unknown type, a missing or malformed limit on a type that needs one, or a where that is not an object of strings and arrays of strings. It never skips a rule it does not understand.

levels.title: Trip totals
levels.brief: Finance also caps what a whole business trip may cost. Add a rule type that adds up the expenses of each trip.
requirements: type "trip_total" with a limit: for each trip, add up the amounts of the trip's expenses that the rule applies to (its where narrows them, e.g. meals only). A trip whose total is over the limit is one violation { ruleId, tripId, expenseIds }, where expenseIds lists every expense of that trip the rule applies to, in input order. Exactly the limit is allowed.
Totals are exact: add up cents, so expenses that add up to exactly the limit are never a violation.
An expense with no tripId belongs to no trip, and trip rules ignore it.
A trip total counts every expense the rule applies to, including expenses that already break another rule (a denied flight still costs the company money until it is sorted out).
For one trip rule, violations come in the order of each trip's first expense in the input. Rule order across types is still the order of the rules list.

levels.title: Daily limits per employee
levels.brief: Some limits are per person per day, like a daily meal allowance while travelling. Add a rule type that adds up each employee's spending on each calendar day.
requirements: type "daily_total" with a limit: for each employee and calendar day, add up the amounts of their expenses the rule applies to. A day whose total is over the limit is one violation { ruleId, employeeId, date, expenseIds }, with date as "YYYY-MM-DD" and expenseIds in input order. Exactly the limit is allowed.

The day is the local date where the expense happened: spentAt is an ISO 8601 time with that place's UTC offset, so the date is the one written in it. "2026-03-02T21:30:00-05:00" is March 2, even though it is March 3 in UTC.
Each employee has their own allowance: two employees on the same trip and day are checked separately. One employee's day counts all of their expenses that day, from any trip or none.
For one daily rule, violations come in the order of each (employee, day)'s first expense in the input.
